```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(qualitychecks)
```

## What this package does

A Fearbase study export bundles two things: the actual **measurement
data** (one row per participant, one column per measure/timepoint/...),
and **metadata** that specifies what was supposed to be collected - which
ratings and questionnaires, how often, with what transformation, and so
on.

`quality_checks()` compares the two. It reads both, and for nine
different aspects of the study (number of participants, participant IDs,
phases, ratings, questionnaires, aggregation, transformation, timepoints,
frequency) checks whether what the metadata *specifies* actually matches
what is *observed* in the data. The result tells you where the two
disagree, so problems can be caught before a dataset is accepted.

## What `quality_checks()` needs

`quality_checks()` takes the path to a directory containing four files:

| File               | Contents                                              |
|--------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| `data_wide.csv`    | The measurement data, one row per participant          |
| `metadata.csv`     | The study's metadata specification                     |
| `study_design.csv` | The study's phases and their timing/trial structure     |
| `codebook.csv`     | The reference codebook of known measure abbreviations   |

In the future, there may be support for a long data format, however, this is
not yet supported.

It also needs reference values for every questionnaire it checks (the
expected number of items, and - for ratings and questionnaires without a
declared aggregation - the plausible value range). These come from a set
of reference tables that ship with the package, so you don't normally
need to supply anything extra:

```{r}
package_dependency_path()
```

You only need to point `quality_checks()` at a different
`dependencies_path` if you're checking a measure the package doesn't
know about yet, or want to try out different reference values for a
specific study - see `?quality_checks` for details. If a questionnaire is
present in your data but missing from these reference tables, the
relevant check fails with a clear message asking you to get in touch
rather than silently giving a wrong answer.

## Running the checks

This package ships a small example study export you can try this out on
right away:

```{r}
example_path <- system.file("extdata", "example", package = "qualitychecks")
list.files(example_path)
```

```{r, message = FALSE}
qc <- quality_checks(example_path)
class(qc)
```

The result is an object of class `quality_checks` - a list with one entry
per check, each carrying its own class so it can be summarised
individually. Printing it with `summary()` gives a compact overview:

```{r}
summary(qc)
```

## Digging into a single check

Each individual check can be summarised on its own, either by pulling it
out of `qc` directly:

```{r}
summary(qc$aggregation)
```

or, equivalently, via `summary(qc, full = TRUE)`, which prints the
detailed summary of every check in one go - useful for a full report, or
when several checks need a closer look at once:

```{r}
summary(qc, full = TRUE)
```

## When a check fails

A failed check means the metadata specification and the observed data
disagree somewhere - not necessarily that the data itself is wrong. See
`vignette("troubleshooting")` for a per-check walkthrough of the most
common reasons a check fails and what to look at first.

## A note on the example data

The bundled example is a synthetic dataset generated to exercise every
check in this package, not real study data. You'll notice the
`participant_id`/`age`/`sex`/`intset` columns end in a run of
underscores (e.g. `participant_id___________`) - that's expected: this
package's variable-naming scheme has twelve underscore-separated slots
(`measure_rangeMin_rangeMax_frequency_transformation_timepoint_day_
phase_block_stimulus_trialNumber_aggregation`), and any slot that doesn't
apply to a given variable is simply left empty, which is what produces
the long underscore runs for variables like `age` that don't carry a
frequency, timepoint, and so on.

You may also see a harmless message like `New names: `` -> `...1`` ` when
`data_wide.csv` is read - this comes from an unnamed leading index column
in the exported CSV and can be ignored.
